title: Beyond Frame Selection: Rethinking Long-Video Understanding with MLLMs

paper.title: Beyond Frame Selection: Rethinking Long-Video Understanding with MLLMs
paper.abstract:
Abstract Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong progress in video understanding, yet it remains challenging because the token limitation makes MLLMs difficult to capture temporally sparse evidence.
Existing methods typically rely on uniform sampling, or frame selection, but these strategies usually optimize either broad temporal coverage or local relevance, making it difficult to preserve both global storyline context and fine-grained evidence.
We propose VideoRouter(VR) that rethinks long-video understanding as coordinating complementary evidence views rather than selecting a single subset of frames . It first organizes each video into a question-agnostic temporal hierarchy, which partition the video into coarse-to-fine temporally coherent segments. In this hierarchy, upper-level nodes capture broad storyline context and event progression, while lower-level nodes preserve fine-grained local details and evidence-bearing moments. This naturally gives rise to two complementary views: a global view for coverage-oriented reasoning and a local view for detail-oriented evidence recovery. We further introduce a verification-guided router to determine which view is better supported by the selected evidence and select the final answer.
We validate the effectiveness of the proposed design through extensive experiments, showing that the verification-guided router effectively coordinates global and local reasoning, and that, on VideoMME, our method outperforms state-of-the-art frame selection methods by 2.9 points, respectively, under the LLaVA-Video-7B backbone. We will release the code.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) Yang et al. (2024) ; Bai et al. (2025b) ; Zhang et al. (2024b) ; Li et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2024a) ; Chen et al. (2024b) ; Nie et al. (2024) have recently made impressive progress in video understanding. However, extending them to long-video understanding remains fundamentally challenging because the visual token budget grows rapidly with video length. For example, if a single frame is represented by roughly 196 visual tokens, then even sampling a video at only 1 frame per second produces 11,760 visual tokens for a one-minute clip and 117,600 tokens for a ten-minute video, far exceeding the context limit of current models. Figure 1: The best local branch is not always the best partner. Using the temporal hierarchy, we fix the global branch and vary the pruning threshold of the shared local branch. The x-axis denotes the strictness of local pruning, with α ∈ { 0.85 , 0.90 , 0.95 } \alpha\in\{0.85,0.90,0.95\} from left to right. For the global branch, Global-U uniformly samples 4 frames from each segment at d rep = 1 d_{\mathrm{rep}}=1 , while Global-C uses the center frame of each segment at the same level. Although Global-U and Global-C use different global sampling strategies, they exhibit a similar trend: stricter local pruning weakens the standalone local branch, yet consistently raises the oracle upper bound. To cope with this challenge, prior work typically compresses the input through uniform sampling or frame selection Tang et al. (2025) ; Liu et al. (2025b) ; Zhang et al. (2025b) ; Zhu et al. (2025) . These strategies, however, optimize different objectives and each leaves a critical gap. Uniform sampling preserves temporal coverage but dilutes the budget over many irrelevant frames, making it weak at capturing fine-grained evidence. Frame selection improves relevance, but often loses the broader temporal context needed for storyline-level understanding. More importantly, evidence in long videos is inherently multi-granular: some questions depend on global event progression, whereas others are determined by short-lived local details. Long-video understanding should therefore not be framed as selecting a single best subset of frames. Instead, it requires coordinating complementary views of evidence.To this end, we propose VideoRouter (VR) , which rethinks long-video understanding as coordinating complementary global and local views rather than selecting a single subset of frames. We first organize each video into a question-agnostic temporal hierarchy that decomposes the video into coarse-to-fine temporally coherent segments. Different levels of this hierarchy naturally support different temporal scopes: higher-level nodes summarize broad story units over long spans, while deeper nodes isolate shorter segments that preserve localized visual evidence. Based on this structure, we construct a global view for storyline coverage and a local view for question-relevant detail recovery. This design also enables a useful analysis of branch interaction. As shown in Figure 1 , under a fixed global branch, stricter local pruning weakens the standalone local branch but increases the oracle upper bound. In other words, a locally stronger branch is not necessarily a better partner for the overall system. What matters is not only branch quality in isolation, but also how much complementary information it contributes. This analysis further supports our formulation that long-video understanding should be addressed by coordinating complementary views rather than selecting a single subset of frames. Once this trade-off is recognized, the key challenge is no longer how to make one branch universally stronger, but how to choose the branch whose evidence granularity best matches the question. Some questions are better served by broad contextual coverage, whereas others require fine-grained local details. We therefore introduce verification-guided routing, which identifies the branch that better satisfies the question’s evidence needs. Extensive experiments on VideoMME Fu et al. (2025) and LongVideoBench Wu et al. (2024) demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework across diverse backbones. Our method consistently outperforms uniform sampling and single-branch reasoning on LongVideoBench, while remaining competitive on VideoMME with less inference frames. These results show that verification-guided routing effectively coordinates complementary global and local evidence rather than relying on either branch alone. Moreover, under the same LLaVA-Video-7B backbone, our method surpasses state-of-the-art frame selection methods on VideoMME by 2.9 points demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed method. Our Contributions are summarized as follows: • We reformulate long-video understanding as coordinating complementary evidence views rather than selecting a single optimal frame subset. We further reveal that a stronger standalone branch may be a worse partner, highlighting cross-view complementarity as a key design objective. • We propose VideoRouter to instantiate this formulation through hierarchy-based global–local evidence construction and evidence-sufficiency routing. It constructs complementary views for broad temporal coverage and fine-grained evidence recovery, and adaptively selects or combines them according to their evidential support. • We validate the effectiveness of the proposed design through extensive experiments. On VideoMME, our method outperforms state-of-the-art frame selection methods by 2.9 under the LLaVA-Video-7B backbone.

sections.heading: 2.1 VideoLLM
sections.text: Following the success of ChatGPT Hurst et al. (2024) , large language models (LLMs) have opened a new era in artificial intelligence. Beyond advances in natural language processing Ouyang et al. (2022) ; Anil et al. (2023) , recent work has extended LLMs to image-language and video-language settings, leading to a series of effective multimodal large language models (MLLMs) Li et al. (2023) ; Ye et al. (2023) ; Chen et al. (2024c) ; Zhang et al. (2024b) ; Li et al. (2024) ; Yang et al. (2024) ; Bai et al. (2025b) ; Cheng et al. (2024) ; Lin et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2024a) ; Chen et al. (2024b) ; Ren et al. (2024) ; Ataallah et al. (2024a) ; Ataallah et al. (2024b) ; Chen et al. (2024a) . Trained on large-scale image-language and video-language data, these models have substantially advanced vision-language understanding. Despite this progress, video MLLMs still face a severe challenge in long-video understanding: their context window remains limited, whereas videos can be far too long to fit within the available token budget. This limitation has motivated a growing body of work on video frame selection and agent-based long-video understanding.

sections.heading: 2.2 Video Frame Selection
sections.text: Due to the limited context window of video MLLMs, a line of work has focused on video frame selection Liu et al. (2025b) ; Tang et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2025b) ; Zhu et al. (2025) . The goal of these methods is to select a small number of informative frames from a long video, so that the MLLM can answer the question with sufficient visual evidence. AKS Tang et al. (2025) proposes Adaptive Keyframe Sampling to balance frame–question relevance and temporal coverage over the video. BOLT Liu et al. (2025b) explores several query-aware frame selection strategies and ultimately adopts inverse transform sampling to select informative frames for long-video understanding. Q-Frame Zhang et al. (2025b) uses the Gumbel-Max trick for efficient frame selection and further adapts the input frame resolution according to similarity scores for better detail understanding.

sections.heading: 2.3 Agent-based Video Understanding
sections.text: Recent work has treated MLLMs as agents that iteratively select useful frames and evaluate intermediate predictions, casting long-video understanding as an interactive multi-step reasoning problem Wang et al. (2024) ; Wang et al. (2025) ; Nie et al. (2024) ; Yang et al. (2025) . VideoAgent Wang et al. (2024) searches for useful frames in a flat frame pool based on frame positions through multi-round reasoning. VideoTree Wang et al. (2025) partitions the video into multiple visually similar clusters and repeatedly queries the MLLM to gather sufficient frames for question answering. VCA Yang et al. (2025) progressively focuses on selected temporal regions to collect frames and answer the question. Beyond multi-round methods, several one-step approaches have also been proposed for long-video understanding Liu et al. (2025c) ; Shen et al. (2025) ; Xie et al. (2025) ; Feng et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2025a) ; Zuo et al. (2025) ; Arnab et al. (2025) ; Luo et al. (2024) . VideoRAG Luo et al. (2024) employs the MLLM as a controller to invoke external tools, such as OCR and audio understanding models, for deeper video analysis. VGent Shen et al. (2025) first constructs a video graph with semantic relationships for efficient frame retrieval, and then reformulates the question into multiple related sentences to reduce retrieval noise. Unlike prior frame selection and agent-based methods, our approach does not formulate long-video understanding as finding a single best subset of frames, either directly or through iterative retrieval. Instead, we organize the video into a temporal hierarchy, derive complementary global and local views from it, and use verification-guided routing to decide which view is better supported for the current question. Our focus is therefore not single-view selection, but adaptive coordination between complementary views.

sections.heading: 3.1 Temporal Hierarchy
sections.text: Long-video evidence naturally exists at multiple temporal granularities: some questions require broad storyline coverage, while others depend on fine-grained local details. To support both, we first organize each video into a question-agnostic hierarchical story structure that provides coarse-to-fine access to temporally coherent content. This hierarchy serves as the common structure for later evidence construction: high-level nodes support global coverage, while low-level nodes preserve detailed visual evidence. In this way, the hierarchy exposes both globally representative frames and fine-grained candidate segments, enabling the later branches to access evidence at the temporal scale required by the question. We then build the temporal hierarchy using contiguous temporal clustering (Pseudu Code is in Append G ). At the first level, we partition the video into M M coarse temporal segments. This coarse partition is designed to preserve broad temporal coverage, and in practice often aligns with major scene or story transitions. Starting from these coarse segments, we recursively split each non-leaf segment into temporally contiguous child segments, producing a coarse-to-fine hierarchy. sections.heading: 3.2 Global Representative Reasoning
sections.text: We first construct a global evidence view to preserve broad temporal coverage of the video. Rather than reasoning over raw frames or uniformly sampled snippets, this branch operates on high-level segments in the story hierarchy, so that the model can access the major temporal units of the video in a compact form. Concretely, for each root-to-leaf path, we select the segment at depth d rep d_{\text{rep}} from the root, where d rep d_{\text{rep}} controls the granularity of the global representation, as illustrated in Figure 2 . If a path is shorter than d rep d_{\text{rep}} , we use its deepest available segment instead. The center frame of each selected segment is then used as its visual representative. Collectively, these representatives form a frame set F g F_{g} that summarizes the video at a coarse yet coverage-preserving level. We then obtain the global prediction by feeding F g F_{g} , together with the question and answer candidates, into the MLLM to obtain answer a g a_{g} for global representative reasoning: a g = MLLM ⁡ ( F g , q , 𝒜 ) . a_{g}=\mathrm{MLLM}(F_{g},q,\mathcal{A}).

sections.heading: 3.3 Local Query-Guided Reasoning
sections.text: To recover fine-grained evidence that may be missed by the global branch, we construct a local evidence view by pruning the story hierarchy toward question-relevant regions. Starting from a lower working level of the tree, our goal is to keep only those temporally coherent segments that contain strong evidence for the current question, while discarding weak or irrelevant branches, as illustrated in Figure 2 . Given the question feature f q f_{q} extracted by the CLIP text encoder Radford et al. (2021) , we assign each segment s s a relevance score based on the most relevant frame it contains: r ⁡ ( s ) = max i ∈ s ⁡ cos ⁡ ( f i , f q ) . r(s)=\max_{i\in s}\cos(f_{i},f_{q}). This max-based definition is appropriate for long-video QA, where decisive evidence is often sparse and may appear in only a small portion of an otherwise long segment. We then define a pruning threshold to decide which segments should be preserved. Specifically, let r max = max s ⁡ r ⁡ ( s ) r_{\max}=\max_{s}r(s) be the highest relevance score among all candidate segments at last level of each root-to-leaf path. We set τ = α ​ r max , \tau=\alpha r_{\max}, where α ∈ ( 0 , 1 ] \alpha\in(0,1] is the prune ratio. Intuitively, this keeps only segments whose relevance is sufficiently close to the strongest candidate at last level of each root-to-leaf path. Segments with r ⁡ ( s ) < τ r(s)<\tau are removed, while segments with r ⁡ ( s ) ≥ τ r(s)\geq\tau are preserved as local evidence candidates. This relative threshold makes the pruning adaptive to each sample, rather than relying on a fixed absolute similarity value. After pruning, we further reduce fragmentation through a roll-up operation. If all original children(before pruning) of a parent segment are retained, we replace them with the parent segment, whose retained score is defined as r ′ ​ ( p ) = max c ∈ Child ⁡ ( p ) ⁡ r ′ ​ ( c ) . r^{\prime}(p)=\max_{c\in\operatorname{Child}(p)}r^{\prime}(c). This preserves the strongest relevance signal while recovering a more coherent temporal unit. Finally, from each retained segment, we uniformly sample 16 frames to form the local evidence set F l F_{l} . The local prediction is then obtained as a l = MLLM ⁡ ( F l , q , 𝒜 ) . a_{l}=\mathrm{MLLM}(F_{l},q,\mathcal{A}).

sections.heading: 3.4 Verification-Guided Routing
sections.text: The global and local branches provide complementary evidence views, but their predictions are not equally reliable for every question. Rather than selecting between them based only on the predicted answer tokens, we explicitly verify whether each prediction is supported by its corresponding selected frames. Specifically, we use an MLLM-based verifier to assess the support level of each branch prediction: s g = Verify ⁡ ( F g , q , 𝒜 , a g ) , s l = Verify ⁡ ( F l , q , 𝒜 , a l ) , s_{g}=\mathrm{Verify}(F_{g},q,\mathcal{A},a_{g}),\qquad s_{l}=\mathrm{Verify}(F_{l},q,\mathcal{A},a_{l}), where s g , s l ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2 } s_{g},s_{l}\in\{0,1,2\} . A score of 2 indicates strong and sufficient visual support for the candidate answer, 1 indicates partial or ambiguous support, and 0 indicates that the evidence does not support the answer, the prompt is in Appendix F . The final decision is made by verification-guided routing. If one branch receives strong support, we trust its prediction. If both branches receive the same non-zero support and agree on the answer, we also accept that answer. All remaining cases are treated as unresolved, indicating that neither branch alone provides sufficiently reliable evidence. For unresolved cases, we concatenate the global and local evidence sets, F u = F g ∪ F l , F_{u}=F_{g}\cup F_{l}, and perform one additional round of reasoning: a u = MLLM ⁡ ( F u , q , 𝒜 ) . a_{u}=\mathrm{MLLM}(F_{u},q,\mathcal{A}). This fallback step combines broad temporal coverage with localized detail, allowing the model to reconsider the question using the union of both evidence views.

sections.heading: Implementation Details.
sections.text: For offline temporal hierarchy construction, we sample each video at 2.0 FPS. In the online stage, the global representative branch uses d rep = 2 d_{\mathrm{rep}}=2 , yielding 32–64 representative center frames per video. As shown in our introduction analysis, although a stricter local threshold slightly weakens the standalone local branch, it yields a higher oracle upper bound by making the local view more complementary to the global branch, so we choose α = 0.95 \alpha=0.95 . For Qwen-based models, the total number of input frames is capped at 128 by uniform subsampling when necessary; for LLaVA-Video, the cap is 64 frames. Unless otherwise specified, the VQA model and the Verification model share the same backbone. All experiments are conducted on NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs. We evaluate on two widely used long-video multiple-choice question answering benchmarks, VideoMME and LongVideoBench. Detailed dataset descriptions are provided in Appendix B .

sections.text: Table 1 compares uniform sampling with our local branch, global branch, verification-guided router, and oracle on VideoMME and LVB. The uniform baseline is reported for reference, for Qwen Bai et al. (2025b) ; Yang et al. (2024) , we uses 128 uniformly sampled frames and 64 uniformly sampled frames for LLaVA-Video Zhang et al. (2024b) . For Qwen2.5-VL, accuracy continues to improve with additional frames within this range, and 128 frames is the largest uniform input supported by our GPU. On VideoMME, the global branch is consistently stronger than the local branch for most models, suggesting that this benchmark benefits more from broad temporal coverage and high-level storyline context. This is most evident for LLaVA-Video-7B, where global reasoning outperforms local reasoning by 4.78 points (64.11 vs. 59.33). Router further improves performance in most cases, reaching the best overall result of 65.52 with Qwen2.5-VL-7B. On LongVideoBench, the trend is reversed. Here, the local branch consistently outperforms the global branch across all backbones, indicating that LVB relies more heavily on fine-grained, question-relevant evidence. Router brings substantial additional gains over both single branches and uniform sampling, improving over uniform by +3.41, +4.07, +8.23, and +6.99 for Qwen2.5-VL-3B, Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and LLaVA-Video-7B, respectively. Overall, the results reveal a clear dataset-dependent preference: VideoMME favors broad global coverage, whereas LVB benefits more from localized, question-guided evidence. Despite this distinction, the proposed router remains competitive on VideoMME while using approximately 50% fewer frames than 128-frame uniform sampling methods, as shown in Appendix Table 9 . Moreover, it consistently achieves the best performance on LongVideoBench across all four evaluated backbones. sections.heading: Comparison with Existing Training-Free Video Agents.
sections.text: Table 3 compares our method with proprietary MLLMs and prior training-free video agents on VideoMME and LVB. Among open 7B-scale training-free methods, both of our variants achieve the strongest results on the two benchmarks. In particular, VideoRouter-Q reaches 65.5 on VideoMME and 64.2 on LVB, outperforming VideoRAG by +3.4 and +5.5 points, respectively. The gains over VideoMind are even larger, reaching +16.3 on VideoMME and +7.9 on LVB. These results show that our global–local evidence construction with verification-guided routing is substantially more effective than prior training-free video agents.

sections.heading: Comparison with Frame Selection Methods.
sections.text: Table 3 further compares our method with adaptive frame selection methods under the same 64-frame budget using LLaVA-Video-7B as the common backbone. Our method again achieves the best performance on both benchmarks, reaching 63.6 on LVB and 64.4 on VideoMME. On LVB, it improves over the LLaVA-Video-7B baseline by +7.0 points, surpasses Q-Frame by +3.7 points, and remains higher than AKS by +1.5 points. On VideoMME, our method improves over the LLaVA-Video-7B baseline by +3.1 points and outperforms AKS by +2.9 points. These results indicate that the improvement does not come merely from selecting better individual frames, but from organizing them into complementary global and local evidence views and resolving them through verification-guided routing.

sections.heading: No-Hierarchy Routing
sections.text: We added a controlled ablation that removes the temporal hierarchy in Figure 3 . The global branch uniformly samples 64 frames because the corresponding hierarchy level contains approximately 64 segment representatives; this matches the global evidence scale while isolating the effect of hierarchical organization. The local branch directly retrieves frames from a flat pool using s i ≥ 0.95 ​ s max s_{i}\geq 0.95s_{\max} . Both branches then use the same verification and fallback pipeline as VideoRouter. This experiment directly covers uniform sampling, flat CLIP retrieval, and routing without hierarchical construction. Under the same routing pipeline, VideoRouter improves over the no-hierarchy router by 4.43 4.43 points and raises the oracle by 1.98 1.98 points, demonstrating the importance of hierarchy-based complementary evidence construction.

sections.heading: Comparison with Lightweight Ensemble Methods
sections.text: We added lightweight alternatives using the same global and local evidence views. Specifically, we evaluate: (1) Next-token confidence , which selects the branch whose predicted answer has the higher next-token probability, following prior work that uses next-token probabilities as a proxy for model confidence Liu et al. (2025a) ; Li et al. (2025) ; (2) Concat , which directly performs one VQA pass over the union of the global and local evidence; (3) Agreement+Concat , which accepts the answer when the two branches agree and otherwise falls back to one VQA pass over their concatenated evidence. Next-token confidence improves over either individual branch, but remains 2.73 2.73 points below verification-guided routing. Concat and Agreement+Concat are stronger alternatives, both reaching 63.10, while verification-guided routing further improves accuracy to 64.23, as in Figure 3 . This result indicates that explicitly assessing whether each prediction is supported by its corresponding visual evidence provides additional information beyond output confidence, evidence concatenation, or branch agreement.

sections.heading: 5 Visualization
sections.text: Figure 4: Qualitative visualization of global–local evidence selection and verification-guided routing. The gray arrow denotes the temporal axis. Local reasoning is more effective for detail-centric questions, while global reasoning is more reliable for questions involving broader event structure. Verification scores help route the final prediction to the better-supported branch. Figure 4 visualizes the frames selected by the global and local branches along the video timeline, together with their predicted answers and verification scores. It illustrates how the two branches attend to different temporal evidence and how routing prefers the branch whose evidence is better supported. In Case 1, the question depends on a fine-grained visual detail: the phone color. The local branch selects frames where this detail is clearly visible and correctly answers red, whereas the global branch samples broader context but does not capture the evidence needed to identify the color, leading to the wrong answer black. Case 2 shows a similar pattern. The answer hinges on the color of the bucket, and the local branch succeeds because it focuses on frames where the bucket is visible, while the global branch misses these evidence-bearing moments and predicts the wrong color. In Case 3, the question instead requires understanding the temporal order of events. Here the global branch captures the overall event progression and predicts the correct sequence, whereas the local branch attends only to partial moments and fails. Overall, the figure shows that local reasoning is more effective when the answer depends on localized visual evidence, while global reasoning is more reliable when broader temporal structure is required. The router then uses the verification scores to select the branch whose prediction is better supported by the selected frames.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we argue that long-video question understanding should not be viewed as selecting a single best subset of frames, but as coordinating complementary evidence across different temporal scales. Based on this perspective, we propose **VideoRouter**, a training-free framework that organizes videos into a question-agnostic temporal hierarchy. This hierarchy supports a global reasoning view for capturing broad storyline context and event progression, as well as a local reasoning view for recovering fine-grained, question-relevant details. VideoRouter further introduces verification-guided routing to evaluate how well each prediction is supported by its visual evidence and to adaptively select or combine the two views. Extensive experiments on VideoMME and LongVideoBench show consistent improvements over single-branch reasoning, frame-selection methods, and prior training-free video agents. These results demonstrate that effective long-video understanding depends not only on finding informative frames, but also on organizing, verifying, and coordinating complementary evidence. We hope this perspective can inspire more reliable, efficient, and flexible long-video reasoning methods for MLLMs.

sections.heading: Appendix B Datasets
sections.text: We evaluate our method on two widely used benchmarks for long-video multiple-choice question answering. VideoMME (w/o sub) Fu et al. (2025) is a human-annotated benchmark containing 900 videos and 2,700 question-answer pairs, with video durations ranging from 11 seconds to 1 hour. It covers 6 domains and 30 fine-grained subcategories, providing a broad evaluation of video understanding ability. Following the w/o sub setting, we evaluate using video frames only, without subtitle input. LongVideoBench(LVB) Wu et al. (2024) is a large-scale benchmark for long-context interleaved video-language understanding. It contains 3,763 web-collected videos and 6,678 human-annotated multiple-choice questions, with video and subtitle inputs of up to one hour. Since our focus is on visual long-video reasoning, we report performance on the official validation set without subtitle input.

sections.heading: C.1 Performance Breakdown by Verification Score Range
sections.text: Table 5 further analyzes routing behavior under different verifier score pairs. Overall, samples with higher verification scores are usually associated with higher accuracy, while lower-score combinations tend to be less reliable, supporting the role of verification as an indicator of evidence quality. On VideoMME, the [ 2 , 2 ] [2,2] group is consistently among the most accurate across all backbones, reaching 72.22 for Qwen-2.5-VL-7B and 68.41 for LLaVA-Video-7B. This suggests that when both branches receive strong support, the selected evidence is usually sufficient for correct answering. By contrast, mixed or low-score groups such as [ 2 , 1 ] [2,1] , [ 1 , 1 ] [1,1] , and [ 1 , 0 ] [1,0] are generally less stable, indicating that these cases remain more ambiguous even when one branch appears moderately confident. Notably, Qwen-2.5-VL-7B still maintains relatively strong performance on [ 1 , 1 ] [1,1] and [ 1 , 0 ] [1,0] , suggesting that a stronger QA backbone can better exploit partially supported evidence. On LVB, the same broad trend holds, but the differences across score ranges are more model-dependent. The [ 2 , 2 ] [2,2] group again performs strongly for all backbones, especially for LLaVA-Video-7B at 69.65. At the same time, some partially supported groups, such as [ 2 , 1 ] [2,1] for Qwen-2-VL-7B (68.42) and [ 1 , 1 ] [1,1] for Qwen-2.5-VL-7B (70.91), also achieve high accuracy. This suggests that on LVB, useful evidence is sometimes captured asymmetrically across the two branches, and that even moderate verification scores can still correspond to correct answers when the retrieved local details are highly relevant. Overall, this analysis supports two conclusions. First, verification scores are informative: strongly supported cases are typically easier and more reliable. Second, the relationship is not strictly monotonic, especially on LVB, where fine-grained evidence may appear in only one branch or only partially satisfy the verifier. This further justifies the need for verification-guided routing rather than relying on a single fixed branch or a hard confidence threshold.

A. 4 women B. 5 women C. 2 women D. 1 woman E. 3 women C C C D Besides hallucination, table 12 summarizes three representative failure categories of the proposed router: subtitle, temporal order, and counting. A common pattern across these cases is that neither the global nor the local branch alone captures sufficiently complete evidence, making final routing inherently difficult. For subtitle questions, the answer depends on precise synchronization between a short-lived visual event and a specific subtitle. In such cases, the global branch often preserves broader context but fails to isolate the exact moment aligned with the target subtitle, while the local branch may focus on visually salient frames that are not temporally aligned with the required subtitle cue. As a result, both branches can appear plausible while still missing the correct text–video correspondence. For temporal order questions, the difficulty lies in recovering the relative order between multiple events rather than identifying a single relevant moment. The global branch may retain broad event progression but miss decisive local transitions, whereas the local branch may capture one or two relevant clips without covering the full event chain. Consequently, the router may receive partial but incomplete support from both branches, which makes reliable selection challenging. Luckily, table 6 shows, increasing frames in Local Branch can solve this problem partially. For counting questions, both branches often suffer from incomplete coverage. The local branch tends to focus on a subset of instances, while the global branch, although broader, may still be too sparse to support accurate counting. In these cases, the failure is not simply that one branch is worse than the other, but that neither branch provides sufficiently exhaustive evidence for an exact numerical answer. Overall, these failures suggest that routing errors often arise not because one branch is clearly superior, but because the required evidence is temporally aligned, sequentially distributed, or globally accumulative in a way that neither branch fully captures.

sections.text: Figure 6: Coarse-to-fine construction of the temporal hierarchy. A video is first partitioned into high-level temporally contiguous segments and then recursively refined into finer sub-segments to expose more detailed structure. Red dashed lines indicate temporal boundaries, and green edges denote parent–child relations. Upper levels capture broad storyline structure, while lower levels preserve more localized event details. Figure 6 illustrates the coarse-to-fine construction of the temporal hierarchy. Starting from the full video, we first obtain a high-level temporal partition, where each segments corresponds to a coarse story unit, such as S 11 S_{11} . The two subscripts indicate the hierarchy level and the segment index within that level, respectively. For example, in S 11 S_{11} , the first subscript 1 1 denotes the first level, and the second subscript 1 1 denotes the first segment at that level. The decomposition is performed recursively using Algorithm 1 , which partitions each non-leaf node into finer temporally contiguous child segments while preserving semantic coherence within each segment. For example, S 11 S_{11} is further decomposed into second-level nodes S 21 S_{21} and S 22 S_{22} . As the hierarchy goes deeper, the segments progressively transition from broad story units to more localized event- and clip-level structures, forming a story–event–clip hierarchy. sections.heading: Appendix E Limitations
sections.text: Despite its effectiveness, our method has several limitations. First, the temporal hierarchy is currently constructed mainly from visual cues. While this is sufficient to provide a useful coarse-to-fine temporal structure, high-level story transitions and event boundaries in long videos are often also signaled by audio and text, such as speech, subtitles, or narration. Incorporating these additional modalities could lead to a more semantically faithful video structure. Second, although the proposed verification-guided router consistently improves over using either branch alone, there remains a noticeable gap between the routed results and the oracle upper bound, indicating that branch coordination is still can be improved. In particular, the current verifier relies on coarse support levels and may struggle on highly ambiguous cases where evidence is partial, subtle, or distributed across both views. Third, our experiments focus on long-video multiple-choice question answering, and it remains to be seen how well the framework generalizes to more open-ended long-video reasoning settings. We view these limitations as promising directions for future work, including query-adaptive video structuring, stronger evidence verification, and broader evaluation beyond multiple-choice QA.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2608.05592v1 [cs.CV] 06 Aug 2026 Beyond Frame Selection: Rethinking Long-Video Understanding with MLLMs Ziling Huang Affiliation: National Institute of Informatics, Japan Shin’ichi Satoh Affiliation: {huangziling, satoh}@nii.ac.jp Abstract Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong progress in video understanding, yet it remains challenging because the token limitation makes MLLMs difficult to capture temporally sparse evidence. Existing methods typically rely on uniform sampling, or frame selection, but these strategies usually optimize either broad temporal coverage or local relevance, making it difficult to preserve both global storyline context and fine-grained evidence. We propose VideoRouter(VR) that rethinks long-video understanding as coordinating complementary evidence views rather than selecting a single subset of frames . It first organizes each video into a question-agnostic temporal hierarchy, which partition the video into coarse-to-fine temporally coherent segments. In this hierarchy, upper-level nodes capture broad storyline context and event progression, while lower-level nodes preserve fine-grained local details and evidence-bearing moments. This naturally gives rise to two complementary views: a global view for coverage-oriented reasoning and a local view for detail-oriented evidence recovery. We further introduce a verification-guided router to determine which view is better supported by the selected evidence and select the final answer. We validate the effectiveness of the proposed design through extensive experiments, showing that the verification-guided router effectively coordinates global and local reasoning, and that, on VideoMME, our method outperforms state-of-the-art frame selection methods by 2.9 points, respectively, under the LLaVA-Video-7B backbone. We will release the code. 1 Introduction Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) Yang et al. (2024) ; Bai et al. (2025b) ; Zhang et al. (2024b) ; Li et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2024a) ; Chen et al. (2024b) ; Nie et al. (2024) have recently made impressive progress in video understanding. However, extending them to long-video understanding remains fundamentally challenging because the visual token budget grows rapidly with video length. For example, if a single frame is represented by roughly 196 visual tokens, then even sampling a video at only 1 frame per second produces 11,760 visual tokens for a one-minute clip and 117,600 tokens for a ten-minute video, far exceeding the context limit of current models. Figure 1: The best local branch is not always the best partner. Using the temporal hierarchy, we fix the global branch and vary the pruning threshold of the shared local branch. The x-axis denotes the strictness of local pruning, with α ∈ { 0.85 , 0.90 , 0.95 } \alpha\in\{0.85,0.90,0.95\} from left to right. For the global branch, Global-U uniformly samples 4 frames from each segment at d rep = 1 d_{\mathrm{rep}}=1 , while Global-C uses the center frame of each segment at the same level. Although Global-U and Global-C use different global sampling strategies, they exhibit a similar trend: stricter local pruning weakens the standalone local branch, yet consistently raises the oracle upper bound. To cope with this challenge, prior work typically compresses the input through uniform sampling or frame selection Tang et al. (2025) ; Liu et al. (2025b) ; Zhang et al. (2025b) ; Zhu et al. (2025) . These strategies, however, optimize different objectives and each leaves a critical gap. Uniform sampling preserves temporal coverage but dilutes the budget over many irrelevant frames, making it weak at capturing fine-grained evidence. Frame selection improves relevance, but often loses the broader temporal context needed for storyline-level understanding. More importantly, evidence in long videos is inherently multi-granular: some questions depend on global event progression, whereas others are determined by short-lived local details. Long-video understanding should therefore not be framed as selecting a single best subset of frames. Instead, it requires coordinating complementary views of evidence.To this end, we propose VideoRouter (VR) , which rethinks long-video understanding as coordinating complementary global and local views rather than selecting a single subset of frames. We first organize each video into a question-agnostic temporal hierarchy that decomposes the video into coarse-to-fine temporally coherent segments. Different levels of this hierarchy naturally support different temporal scopes: higher-level nodes summarize broad story units over long spans, while deeper nodes isolate shorter segments that preserve localized visual evidence. Based on this structure, we construct a global view for storyline coverage and a local view for question-relevant detail recovery. This design also enables a useful analysis of branch interaction. As shown in Figure 1 , under a fixed global branch, stricter local pruning weakens the standalone local branch but increases the oracle upper bound. In other words, a locally stronger branch is not necessarily a better partner for the overall system. What matters is not only branch quality in isolation, but also how much complementary information it contributes. This analysis further supports our formulation that long-video understanding should be addressed by coordinating complementary views rather than selecting a single subset of frames. Once this trade-off is recognized, the key challenge is no longer how to make one branch universally stronger, but how to choose the branch whose evidence granularity best matches the question. Some questions are better served by broad contextual coverage, whereas others require fine-grained local details. We therefore introduce verification-guided routing, which identifies the branch that better satisfies the question’s evidence needs. Extensive experiments on VideoMME Fu et al. (2025) and LongVideoBench Wu et al. (2024) demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework across diverse backbones. Our method consistently outperforms uniform sampling and single-branch reasoning on LongVideoBench, while remaining competitive on VideoMME with less inference frames. These results show that verification-guided routing effectively coordinates complementary global and local evidence rather than relying on either branch alone. Moreover, under the same LLaVA-Video-7B backbone, our method surpasses state-of-the-art frame selection methods on VideoMME by 2.9 points demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed method. Our Contributions are summarized as follows: • We reformulate long-video understanding as coordinating complementary evidence views rather than selecting a single optimal frame subset. We further reveal that a stronger standalone branch may be a worse partner, highlighting cross-view complementarity as a key design objective. • We propose VideoRouter to instantiate this formulation through hierarchy-based global–local evidence construction and evidence-sufficiency routing. It constructs complementary views for broad temporal coverage and fine-grained evidence recovery, and adaptively selects or combines them according to their evidential support. • We validate the effectiveness of the proposed design through extensive experiments. On VideoMME, our method outperforms state-of-the-art frame selection methods by 2.9 under the LLaVA-Video-7B backbone. 2 Related Works 2.1 VideoLLM Following the success of ChatGPT Hurst et al. (2024) , large language models (LLMs) have opened a new era in artificial intelligence. Beyond advances in natural language processing Ouyang et al. (2022) ; Anil et al. (2023) , recent work has extended LLMs to image-language and video-language settings, leading to a series of effective multimodal large language models (MLLMs) Li et al. (2023) ; Ye et al. (2023) ; Chen et al. (2024c) ; Zhang et al. (2024b) ; Li et al. (2024) ; Yang et al. (2024) ; Bai et al. (2025b) ; Cheng et al. (2024) ; Lin et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2024a) ; Chen et al. (2024b) ; Ren et al. (2024) ; Ataallah et al. (2024a) ; Ataallah et al. (2024b) ; Chen et al. (2024a) . Trained on large-scale image-language and video-language data, these models have substantially advanced vision-language understanding. Despite this progress, video MLLMs still face a severe challenge in long-video understanding: their context window remains limited, whereas videos can be far too long to fit within the available token budget. This limitation has motivated a growing body of work on video frame selection and agent-based long-video understanding. 2.2 Video Frame Selection Due to the limited context window of video MLLMs, a line of work has focused on video frame selection Liu et al. (2025b) ; Tang et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2025b) ; Zhu et al. (2025) . The goal of these methods is to select a small number of informative frames from a long video, so that the MLLM can answer the question with sufficient visual evidence. AKS Tang et al. (2025) proposes Adaptive Keyframe Sampling to balance frame–question relevance and temporal coverage over the video. BOLT Liu et al. (2025b) explores several query-aware frame selection strategies and ultimately adopts inverse transform sampling to select informative frames for long-video understanding. Q-Frame Zhang et al. (2025b) uses the Gumbel-Max trick for efficient frame selection and further adapts the input frame resolution according to similarity scores for better detail understanding. 2.3 Agent-based Video Understanding Recent work has treated MLLMs as agents that iteratively select useful frames and evaluate intermediate predictions, casting long-video understanding as an interactive multi-step reasoning problem Wang et al. (2024) ; Wang et al. (2025) ; Nie et al. (2024) ; Yang et al. (2025) . VideoAgent Wang et al. (2024) searches for useful frames in a flat frame pool based on frame positions through multi-round reasoning. VideoTree Wang et al. (2025) partitions the video into multiple visually similar clusters and repeatedly queries the MLLM to gather sufficient frames for question answering. VCA Yang et al. (2025) progressively focuses on selected temporal regions to collect frames and answer the question. Beyond multi-round methods, several one-step approaches have also been proposed for long-video understanding Liu et al. (2025c) ; Shen et al. (2025) ; Xie et al. (2025) ; Feng et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2025a) ; Zuo et al. (2025) ; Arnab et al. (2025) ; Luo et al. (2024) . VideoRAG Luo et al. (2024) employs the MLLM as a controller to invoke external tools, such as OCR and audio understanding models, for deeper video analysis. VGent Shen et al. (2025) first constructs a video graph with semantic relationships for efficient frame retrieval, and then reformulates the question into multiple related sentences to reduce retrieval noise. Unlike prior frame selection and agent-based methods, our approach does not formulate long-video understanding as finding a single best subset of frames, either directly or through iterative retrieval. Instead, we organize the video into a temporal hierarchy, derive complementary global and local views from it, and use verification-guided routing to decide which view is better supported for the current question. Our focus is therefore not single-view selection, but adaptive coordination between complementary views. 3 VideoRouter Figure 2: Overview of the proposed VideoRouter. The input video is first organized into a temporal hierarchy, where each s s represents a segment containing multiple frames. For clarity, the illustration shows the full video being divided into two coarse segments at the first layer; in practice, however, the first layer typically contains around 32 coarse segments. Based on this hierarchy, we derive a global representative evidence set F g F_{g} and a local query-guided evidence set F l F_{l} . The two branches perform VQA independently and are further assessed by a verification model. Verification-guided routing either accepts a sufficiently supported branch prediction or invokes an additional reasoning pass on the union of both evidence sets. We consider multiple-choice video question answering, where the input consists of a video V V , a question q q , and a set of candidate answers 𝒜 = { a 1 , … , a T } \mathcal{A}=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{T}\} . The goal is to predict the correct answer a ∗ ∈ 𝒜 a_{*}\in\mathcal{A} . The framework is shown in Figure 2 . 3.1 Temporal Hierarchy Long-video evidence naturally exists at multiple temporal granularities: some questions require broad storyline coverage, while others depend on fine-grained local details. To support both, we first organize each video into a question-agnostic hierarchical story structure that provides coarse-to-fine access to temporally coherent content. This hierarchy serves as the common structure for later evidence construction: high-level nodes support global coverage, while low-level nodes preserve detailed visual evidence. In this way, the hierarchy exposes both globally representative frames and fine-grained candidate segments, enabling the later branches to access evidence at the temporal scale required by the question. Given a video V = { v 1 , … , v t } V=\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{t}\} , we first extract a visual feature f i f_{i} for each sampled frame using a CLIP visual encoder ϕ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \phi(\cdot) Radford et al. (2021) : f i = ϕ ( v i ) ∈ ℝ d , i = 1 , … , t . f_{i}=\phi(v_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\quad i=1,\ldots,t. We then build the temporal hierarchy using contiguous temporal clustering (Pseudu Code is in Append G ). At the first level, we partition the video into M M coarse temporal segments. This coarse partition is designed to preserve broad temporal coverage, and in practice often aligns with major scene or story transitions. Starting from these coarse segments, we recursively split each non-leaf segment into temporally contiguous child segments, producing a coarse-to-fine hierarchy. The recursion stops when the segment length falls below a predefined threshold L leaf L_{\text{leaf}} =16, so that deeper nodes correspond to increasingly localized temporal details(Details are in Append D ). For each s s , we additionally define a representative center frame, which is later used by the representative branch. Specifically, we compute the mean feature of frames in segment and select the frame with the highest cosine similarity to it: f ¯ s = 1 | s | ​ ∑ i ∈ s f i , c ⁡ ( s ) = arg ⁡ max i ∈ s ⁡ cos ⁡ ( f i , f ¯ s ) . \bar{f}_{s}=\frac{1}{|s|}\sum_{i\in s}f_{i},\qquad c(s)=\arg\max_{i\in s}\cos(f_{i},\bar{f}_{s}). This center frame provides a compact visual anchor for the segments. 3.2 Global Representative Reasoning We first construct a global evidence view to preserve broad temporal coverage of the video. Rather than reasoning over raw frames or uniformly sampled snippets, this branch operates on high-level segments in the story hierarchy, so that the model can access the major temporal units of the video in a compact form. Concretely, for each root-to-leaf path, we select the segment at depth d rep d_{\text{rep}} from the root, where d rep d_{\text{rep}} controls the granularity of the global representation, as illustrated in Figure 2 . If a path is shorter than d rep d_{\text{rep}} , we use its deepest available segment instead. The center frame of each selected segment is then used as its visual representative. Collectively, these representatives form a frame set F g F_{g} that summarizes the video at a coarse yet coverage-preserving level. We then obtain the global prediction by feeding F g F_{g} , together with the question and answer candidates, into the MLLM to obtain answer a g a_{g} for global representative reasoning: a g = MLLM ⁡ ( F g , q , 𝒜 ) . a_{g}=\mathrm{MLLM}(F_{g},q,\mathcal{A}). 3.3 Local Query-Guided Reasoning To recover fine-grained evidence that may be missed by the global branch, we construct a local evidence view by pruning the story hierarchy toward question-relevant regions. Starting from a lower working level of the tree, our goal is to keep only those temporally coherent segments that contain strong evidence for the current question, while discarding weak or irrelevant branches, as illustrated in Figure 2 . Given the question feature f q f_{q} extracted by the CLIP text encoder Radford et al. (2021) , we assign each segment s s a relevance score based on the most relevant frame it contains: r ⁡ ( s ) = max i ∈ s ⁡ cos ⁡ ( f i , f q ) . r(s)=\max_{i\in s}\cos(f_{i},f_{q}). This max-based definition is appropriate for long-video QA, where decisive evidence is often sparse and may appear in only a small portion of an otherwise long segment. We then define a pruning threshold to decide which segments should be preserved. Specifically, let r max = max s ⁡ r ⁡ ( s ) r_{\max}=\max_{s}r(s) be the highest relevance score among all candidate segments at last level of each root-to-leaf path. We set τ = α ​ r max , \tau=\alpha r_{\max}, where α ∈ ( 0 , 1 ] \alpha\in(0,1] is the prune ratio. Intuitively, this keeps only segments whose relevance is sufficiently close to the strongest candidate at last level of each root-to-leaf path. Segments with r ⁡ ( s ) < τ r(s)<\tau are removed, while segments with r ⁡ ( s ) ≥ τ r(s)\geq\tau are preserved as local evidence candidates. This relative threshold makes the pruning adaptive to each sample, rather than relying on a fixed absolute similarity value. After pruning, we further reduce fragmentation through a roll-up operation. If all original children(before pruning) of a parent segment are retained, we replace them with the parent segment, whose retained score is defined as r ′ ​ ( p ) = max c ∈ Child ⁡ ( p ) ⁡ r ′ ​ ( c ) . r^{\prime}(p)=\max_{c\in\operatorname{Child}(p)}r^{\prime}(c). This preserves the strongest relevance signal while recovering a more coherent temporal unit. Finally, from each retained segment, we uniformly sample 16 frames to form the local evidence set F l F_{l} . The local prediction is then obtained as a l = MLLM ⁡ ( F l , q , 𝒜 ) . a_{l}=\mathrm{MLLM}(F_{l},q,\mathcal{A}). 3.4 Verification-Guided Routing The global and local branches provide complementary evidence views, but their predictions are not equally reliable for every question. Rather than selecting between them based only on the predicted answer tokens, we explicitly verify whether each prediction is supported by its corresponding selected frames. Specifically, we use an MLLM-based verifier to assess the support level of each branch prediction: s g = Verify ⁡ ( F g , q , 𝒜 , a g ) , s l = Verify ⁡ ( F l , q , 𝒜 , a l ) , s_{g}=\mathrm{Verify}(F_{g},q,\mathcal{A},a_{g}),\qquad s_{l}=\mathrm{Verify}(F_{l},q,\mathcal{A},a_{l}), where s g , s l ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2 } s_{g},s_{l}\in\{0,1,2\} . A score of 2 indicates strong and sufficient visual support for the candidate answer, 1 indicates partial or ambiguous support, and 0 indicates that the evidence does not support the answer, the prompt is in Appendix F . The final decision is made by verification-guided routing. If one branch receives strong support, we trust its prediction. If both branches receive the same non-zero support and agree on the answer, we also accept that answer. All remaining cases are treated as unresolved, indicating that neither branch alone provides sufficiently reliable evidence. For unresolved cases, we concatenate the global and local evidence sets, F u = F g ∪ F l , F_{u}=F_{g}\cup F_{l}, and perform one additional round of reasoning: a u = MLLM ⁡ ( F u , q , 𝒜 ) . a_{u}=\mathrm{MLLM}(F_{u},q,\mathcal{A}). This fallback step combines broad temporal coverage with localized detail, allowing the model to reconsider the question using the union of both evidence views. 4 Experiments 4.1 Experiments Setups Implementation Details. For offline temporal hierarchy construction, we sample each video at 2.0 FPS. In the online stage, the global representative branch uses d rep = 2 d_{\mathrm{rep}}=2 , yielding 32–64 representative center frames per video. As shown in our introduction analysis, although a stricter local threshold slightly weakens the standalone local branch, it yields a higher oracle upper bound by making the local view more complementary to the global branch, so we choose α = 0.95 \alpha=0.95 . For Qwen-based models, the total number of input frames is capped at 128 by uniform subsampling when necessary; for LLaVA-Video, the cap is 64 frames. Unless otherwise specified, the VQA model and the Verification model share the same backbone. All experiments are conducted on NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs. We evaluate on two widely used long-video multiple-choice question answering benchmarks, VideoMME and LongVideoBench. Verification scores help route the final prediction to the better-supported branch. Figure 4 visualizes the frames selected by the global and local branches along the video timeline, together with their predicted answers and verification scores. It illustrates how the two branches attend to different temporal evidence and how routing prefers the branch whose evidence is better supported. In Case 1, the question depends on a fine-grained visual detail: the phone color. The local branch selects frames where this detail is clearly visible and correctly answers red, whereas the global branch samples broader context but does not capture the evidence needed to identify the color, leading to the wrong answer black. Case 2 shows a similar pattern. The answer hinges on the color of the bucket, and the local branch succeeds because it focuses on frames where the bucket is visible, while the global branch misses these evidence-bearing moments and predicts the wrong color. In Case 3, the question instead requires understanding the temporal order of events. Here the global branch captures the overall event progression and predicts the correct sequence, whereas the local branch attends only to partial moments and fails. Overall, the figure shows that local reasoning is more effective when the answer depends on localized visual evidence, while global reasoning is more reliable when broader temporal structure is required. The router then uses the verification scores to select the branch whose prediction is better supported by the selected frames. 6 Conclusion In this paper, we argue that long-video question understanding should not be viewed as selecting a single best subset of frames, but as coordinating complementary evidence across different temporal scales. Based on this perspective, we propose **VideoRouter**, a training-free framework that organizes videos into a question-agnostic temporal hierarchy. This hierarchy supports a global reasoning view for capturing broad storyline context and event progression, as well as a local reasoning view for recovering fine-grained, question-relevant details. VideoRouter further introduces verification-guided routing to evaluate how well each prediction is supported by its visual evidence and to adaptively select or combine the two views. Extensive experiments on VideoMME and LongVideoBench show consistent improvements over single-branch reasoning, frame-selection methods, and prior training-free video agents. These results demonstrate that effective long-video understanding depends not only on finding informative frames, but also on organizing, verifying, and coordinating complementary evidence. We hope this perspective can inspire more reliable, efficient, and flexible long-video reasoning methods for MLLMs. References Anil et al.
